reviewEvidence.visualReviewMethod: Full-duration six-second contact sheets inspected; transform definitions, bounce A/B, Game Boy Kirby, simple oval versus corrected silhouette, blend-shape card and Mario fist example reviewed. Not continuous audio or every-frame review.
reviewEvidence.resolutionNote: Research-only reference media; never a production source. Independent production footage still requires genuine FHD or higher.

centralQuestion: How can changing a character's shape make the same motion feel softer, livelier and more substantial?
thesis: Use scaling and squash-and-stretch to change the perceived material and energy of motion, maintain convincing visual volume, and use more deliberate shape deformation when simple scaling produces a weak silhouette.

claims: Scaling, rotation and translation are fundamental object transforms.
Translation and rotation are common animation tools, but scaling also deserves deliberate use.
sections.observedVisuals: Three colour-coded cubes illustrate size, rotation and movement.
additionalPrerequisites: Show size, direction and position changing separately before naming their technical transforms.
sections.ownScreenProposal: One object on the grid, one transform at a time, with canonical English/Korean term and a compact value label. A cube is appropriate as a geometric transform object; use a recognisable rig for later character demonstrations.
sections.transitionToNext: Keep the object's route unchanged and add only scaling to reveal what this third transform contributes.

claims: A bouncing ball without deformation can work, but squash and stretch changes its perceived texture and liveliness.
Squash and Stretch names the coordinated flattening and elongation used for this effect.
sections.observedVisuals: Bouncing-ball animation without deformation, then with deformation, then side-by-side comparison.
exampleRoles: A controlled ball bounce isolates shape change from the movement path.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Same bounce path, height, timing and contact moment on the same grid; only scale curves differ. Explain the visible flattening at contact and elongation in motion while they happen.
sections.transitionToNext: The shape can change strongly while still looking like the same amount of material.

sections.role: Preserve volume rather than simply shrink
claims: When compressing vertically, compensate by expanding in another direction so the object keeps a convincing sense of volume.
This is an artistic volume-preservation guideline, not a claim that changing Transform scale updates physics mass.
sections.observedVisuals: Ball flattened vertically and widened horizontally with directional arrows.
sections.correction: The source narration/caption calls this keeping mass roughly constant. In a geometric demonstration, call the controlled quantity visible volume (or area for a 2D drawing), and distinguish it from physical mass. Preserve the intended lesson rather than repeating an ambiguous physical claim.
additionalPrerequisites: For a 2D worked illustration, scale width by 2 and height by 1/2 so the area multiplier stays 1. For a 3D object with depth unchanged, the same x/y pair also preserves volume. If both horizontal axes expand equally, explain why their factors differ.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Add width × height × depth multipliers beside the same object and substitute simple numbers; label a flat drawing's calculation as area, not volume.
sections.transitionToNext: Even when the amount of visible material feels consistent, the contour itself may still need a more specific shape.

claims: Kirby's crouch and landing deform the body, including the early Game Boy depiction.
A 3D body flattened by simple scaling can feel less substantial than the intended sprite shape.
The desired squashed silhouette has fuller sides, closer to a rounded track-like outline than an ordinary flattened ellipse.
sections.observedVisuals: Game Boy crouch/landing, plain oval diagram, internal comparison of non-final 3D Kirby and pixel art, then modern Smash Kirby.
exampleRoles: Sprite-to-model comparison demonstrates why a shape's contour matters beyond its overall bounding dimensions.
sections.retainedTeaching: Keep the distinct fuller-edge silhouette problem, not merely another generic squash example. The historical internal report is attribution only; the visible design issue can be independently explained.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Independently sourced FHD Kirby footage for the real result; our own rounded character on the grid compares scale-only deformation with a deliberately shaped contour. Never reuse the source's non-final internal assets or report image.
sections.transitionToNext: Changing the actual shape, rather than only its overall scale, gives another implementation route.

sections.role: Blend shape as a possible route, not an asserted game implementation
claims: A blend shape can interpolate vertex positions toward a designed target shape.
This can add fuller sides that global scaling alone does not produce.
The source discusses blend shapes as an idea and explicitly does not confirm which final implementation was used for Kirby.
sections.observedVisuals: Blend-shape definition card and Kirby's changing shape.
additionalPrerequisites: Define mesh vertex as a point in the surface and target shape as another arrangement of corresponding points. Show a few matched vertices before introducing the full smooth body.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Our labelled implementation changes blend-shape weight from 0 to 1 while preserving matched vertex identities; show the changed side contour. Do not label the demonstration Kirby's engine technique.
sections.transitionToNext: These shape changes can be subtle, but they are distinct from enlarging a body part simply to emphasise an attack.

sections.role: Distinguish deformation feel from simple exaggeration
claims: Scale animation appears in small character details.
Mario's enlarged punching fist is an exaggeration example, distinct from the material/volume-focused squash-and-stretch discussion.
sections.observedVisuals: Mario's fist marked before/after with arrows during a punch.
sections.retainedTeaching: Keep this distinction; do not call every scale change squash and stretch or imply every exaggeration must preserve volume.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Show independent Mario evidence if available and a clearly authored enlarged-fist illustration beside the earlier same-volume bounce, identifying their different purposes.
sections.transitionToNext: Choose the shape technique according to the feeling the movement needs.

claims: Consider scale and shape animation when movement lacks energy or material character.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Replay the same bounce and character landing with the final shape choices, preserving the comparison and labels rather than adding a new topic.

evidence.support: SideFX describes squash/stretch as representing volume preservation.
Toon Boom teaches maintaining the object's volume through squash and stretch.
Unity describes blend-shape vertex deltas and indexed vertex data, with interpolation between shapes.
SideFX describes shape blending for corresponding topology.

technicalClarifications.scope: Our demonstration must keep corresponding vertices; same vertex count alone does not guarantee that arbitrary unrelated models form a useful blend shape. No inference about Kirby's actual implementation.
